Anticomplementary Triangle

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Move the three corners of a triangle and watch the other triangles follow them.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to name the points or to light up each building step.
Look for the math

Start with any triangle and build two rounds of equilateral triangles on its sides. The last triangle you get is not just similar to the first: the three corners you started with sit exactly at the middles of its sides. Drag a corner and see if you can break that.

Two rounds of equilateral triangles

On the sides of ABC put ABZ, BCX and CAY, all turned the same way: those are the red points. This is the first half of Napoleon's theorem. Now turn the other way on the sides of XYZ to get XYR, YZP and ZXQ: those are the green points P, Q, R. Tick "first step" and "second step" to see the two rounds one at a time.

Add the corners like numbers

A turn of 60° is multiplication by c = (1 + i√3) / 2 in complex numbers. So the first round gives X = (1 − c)B + cC, Y = (1 − c)C + cA, Z = (1 − c)A + cB. The opposite turn on the second round gives P = (1 − c)Z + cY, and the same pattern for Q and R. These are exactly the rotations the old Java applet performed.

The surprise falls out

Substitute one line into the next. Because (1 − c)2 + c2 = −1 and c(1 − c) = 1, everything cancels to P = −A + B + C, Q = A − B + C and R = A + B − C. Then Q − P = 2(A − B): side PQ is parallel to AB and twice as long, and (P + Q) / 2 = C. The same holds at the other two corners, so ABC is the medial triangle of PQR and the green triangle has four times its area.

What was checked

The logic test checks all of those claims on the starting triangle, seven hand-picked shapes and 600 random ones, and compares every point with both the article's complex formulas and the applet's own rotation method. It also checks the two rounds of triangles are equilateral and that the second round turns opposite to the first. One small wording detail: the article says the first three triangles have "similarly oriented" equilateral triangles. That means they match each other and the second round is opposite to them; it is not tied to which way ABC itself is drawn. The old Java applet is not embedded on its short droodle page any more — the theorem, proof and a newer interactive version are on the explanation page.

Drag C across the line AB. The starting triangle now winds the other way, but the two building rounds keep their turns and A, B, C still sit at the middles of the green sides.
